Day is Friday, November 24, and preceding this the armual Convention will
be held on November 22 and 23, so that a three day memorable session will
attract many hundreds of alumni and undergraduates to old Union College.
The detailed program of the three days events will reach every alumnus
of the Fraternity early next fall. We are withholding this specific data
during the general vacation season, pending its final completion as a formal
program. For several months the Executive Council and the Centennial
Committee of the Theta Chapter have been at work on the program, and by
September 15 all arrangements will be completed and an intense drive made
to secure a large and representative attendance.

Joseph B. Eastman, Gamma '04 has been mentioned most frequently

"EASTMAN, COMMISSIONER, DISSENTS."
This meticulous sentence began to appear in the reports of the Inter
state Commerce Commission in 1919. During the intervening 14 years, the
dissenting opinions of Joseph Bartlett Eastman have come to occupy a posi
tion in the world of transportation comparable to those of Justice Brandeis
in the realm of the law.

Dissenting opinions, as a rule, are interesting and informative but un
important, because the majority opinion of any tribunal rules though rendered
by however close a margin. But the dissenting opinions of Commissioner
Eastman have acquired unusual power, not
infrequently they have been
upheld in the courts; they are generally regarded as the progressive dictum
on
problems of transportation and the public interest therein.

GRIM, BUT GRINS

You might well expect a man, whose blistering dissents on
railway prob
lems have burned a definite path for railway legislation, to be a grim old

THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON 229

cuss. But here Joe Eastman would fool you. For, while 51, he looks much
younger and his face breaks readily into a friendly grin.
Eastman is a gentle person, who likes to fish and to play squash, but
who minces no words in telling railway magnates when to put on the brakes.
And while Eastman makes news when he writes a dissenting opinion in
a big Interstate Conunerce Commission case, he probably would like to be
known also for his majority views. As a matter of record, when President
Roosevelt mapped his railroad program, it was Eastman he called in from
the I. C. C. to help. There were those who suspected that Eastman consulted
with the President before the latter made his Salt Lake City railroad speech.
This was not the case, but the similarity of views is marked. President
Roosevelt, in seeking his advice later, evidently recognized this.
His friends recall that President Wilson in sending Eastman's appoint
ment to the Senate, identified him as a Republican from Massachusetts; and

that the appointee immediately wrote his senatorial friends that he was
an independent, and wanted to be appointed and confirmed as such. He was.
He still is.

CALLED "radical"

This independence has caused Eastman to be damned as "radical" by
some railway managers. He believes, for instance, the time will come when
the government will have to operate the railroads and other public utilities.
He has never crusaded for these ideas ; he has simply stated them when called
upon.
Some of his best friends are railroad executives. They disagree more
often than they agree with him, but at the same time they acknowledge his

deep fund of information, his fairness, his intelligence.
Bureaucracy's evils always have impressed him. In a relatively un
important case involving distribution of freight cars in Nebraska back in
1919, he said: "It is highly desirable, if undue centralization and concen
tration of governmental powers in Washington are to be avoided, that every

question should be left to the disposition of state authorities which can
reasonably and with a proper regard for the general public interest be dealt
with in that way."
You run across that phrase "a proper regard for the general public
interest" often in his opinions.
He early had a clear idea of what the Interstate Commerce Commission
look for. "I cannot but believe," he said

A NEW METHOD IN COLLEGE
FINANCING
BY RALPH S. CLARK, ROLLINS COLLEGE*

job of financing a college has whitened the hair of many a presi

THE dent, and driven them, prematurely, to their graves. Many of them
have become nothing less than "glorified panhandlers" in their efforts,
at the end of the fiscal year, to bridge the ever-widening gap between expendi

tures and income. Happy is the lot of the college president who does not
see "red" on the ledger on June 30.

What is the reason for this discrepancy between income and outgo ? Who
pays the bills of education in this country, anyhow?
More than one million students went to college last year. The educa
tional bill for the colleges, universities and technical schools amounted last
year to more than five hundred million dollars. Who paid?
One of the favorite indoor sports of college fiscal agents is to figure the
difference between what a student pays to a college for tuition, board and room
and what it is costing the college for the student's instruction, board and
room. The margin vari^; but statistics are available which prove that the
students pay only about half of what the colleges are spending.
Part of this difference in most institutions is made up by income from
accumulated endowment. Another part, politely called "annual deficit," is
made up, to some extent, by gifts from friends. The usual procedure in
securing this relief is for the president to "pass the hat." And in many institu
tions the difference is never made up and colleges go on aimlessly piling up
deficit after deficit until the sheriff casts his shadow across the portals of the
"administration building."
Perhaps the greatest evil connected with college financing is the use of
endowment income to eke out student income without making distinction be
tween the well-to-do student and the poor student as far as the benefits of the
endowment funds are concerned.
When a donor gives a sum of, say, $1,000,000 to a college for endowment,
the income from this endowment, about $50,000, is lumped, indiscriminately,
as general income, unless otherwise restricted, and the benefit derived from

this endowment income is distributed, equally, to every student in the college.

Thus the son of a millionaire gets a certain unit of benefit from this income
no less in degree than the son of a laborer.
John D. Rockefeller, Jr., in an address delivered at Brown University, in
1927, pointed to this difficulty in the misuse of endowment income in a frank
discussion of college tuition fees.
"The privately supported colleges in this country," said Mr. Rockefeller,
"were originally founded as charitable institutions, with the expectation that

they would be maintained by contributions of philanthropic people. A col
lege education was practically free, for it was assumed that the students bene
fitting therefrom would go into the ministry, into teaching or engagement in
some other professional activity in which the financial returns to them would

be small but the gain to the public large. Under the conditions which then
existed, the proposition was logical. Today, however, the majority of the
students go to college for a good time, for social considerations or to fit them
selves to earn money. The idea of service to thei community is no longer the
chief consideration. It would seem, therefore, that imder these changed
conditions the student might properly be expected to pay for the benefits he
receives."
Referring to a report issued by the Bureau of Education showing the
receipts of privately supported colleges and universities during the year
1923-24, Mr. Rockefeller showed that about one-half of the total income came
from student fees, one-quarter from endowment, and one-quarter from gifts
and other sources. This evidence shows that the student pays only a half of the
actual cost to the college of his education.
"Colleges and universities are confronted with the necessity of securing
either scores of additional millions for endowment or increased current in
come," said Mr. Rockefeller. But that these vast sums can be secured from pri
vate sources in addition to all that has been given during the past ten years is, he

believes, "hardly probable." And he asks, "Where then shall college and uni
versity fiscal officers look for the large added income that must be secured?"
Rollins College has answered this question by adopting the Unit-Cost
Plan which marks a radical departure from the conventional method of
financing a college.
The Unit-Cost Plan, conceived by President Hamilton Holt and adopted
by the Board of Trustees after several years of study, becomes effective in the
fall of 1933. It is plan at once simple, scientific, and concrete. It is
a

commended to any other institution whose officers feel that a new philosophy
in college financing is demanded by the transmutation in the industrial
and

social life of the nation.

In brief the plan is this:

(a) The plan budgets the operating expenses of the College on an
adequate but not an extravagant basis.
(b) It divides the annual operating expenses of the College by the
estimated student enrollment, which is limited to five hundred.

(c) It then fixes the cost of board, room and tuition of the individual
students as one unit cost of the total, which, it is calculated, will be $1350 for
the next year.

(d) It makes available the income of present endowment, approxi
mately $60,000 a year, plus any gifts which may be received for loans or
scholarships, for reducing tuition to those worthy and desirable students who
can show that they cannot pay the entire cost.
This Unit-Cost Plan will apply to all students except:

(1) Those whose parents are actual residents of the College commimity.
Such students, who maintain approved academic standards, will be granted a
limited number of partial scholarships in recognition of the friendship and
support of the community which serves us and which we try to serve.

(2) Those students of approved standing now at Rollins who can show
that they will have to leave college if they are required to pay the entire cost.
Under the Unit-Cost Plan separate charges will not be made for tuition,
board and room. Instead, each student will be expected to pay in three in
stallments the sum of $1350, which represents one unit cost of the armual
expense of operating the college on its present basis of efficiency, and with its
present student body.
So far as known, Rollins is the first college to ask all of its students who
are
financially able to do so to pay the actual cost of their education, and
devote the entire income from its endowment to scholarship aid. This
plan
puts Rollins on an honest, self-respecting and sound plan, both financially and
philosophically.
There seems to be no fear among President Holt and his associates that
the Unit-Cost Plan will make Rollins a rich man's college. Even with the
increased tuition, it is argued, the costs of graduation will be less than that
of many standard colleges throughout the country. And, with a minimum of
$60,000 a year available for scholarships a sum which will be increased,

unquestionably, by gifts from time to time Rollins expects to retain a happy

balance between the number of the "rich" students and the number of socalled "poor" students.

While the Unit-Cost Plan is devised
chiefly to distribute costs more
equitably and to equalize opportunity, the trustees are working out a number
of improvements for inauguration next fall, among which is a
housing system
whereby the living accommodations of students, in fraternities and dormi
tories, will be more nearly uniform, and whereby all special fees and tuition
charges for individual instruction, especially in the art, dramatic and music
departments, will be eliminated so that a student will not be prevented from
taking such courses as in the past, on account of extra fees.
It should be especially emphasized that this plan does not
contemplate
applying any of the endowment income or student fees for new buildings.
The trustees still think the services of Rollins College to
society justify out
side contributions for capital improvements. It should be
equally emphasized
that any further addition to scholarship, loan, or specified endowment funds
will be made available to students who cannot pay the full cost of tuition.
The Unit-Cost Plan is the third noteworthy step Rollins has taken in its
progressive educational development.
The Conference Plan, adopted seven years ago to humanize methods of
instruction, discarded the prevailing lecture-recitation system of teaching
in which the professor was active and the student passive, and made learning
a joint adventure on the
part of the professor and student. Under the
Conference Plan the lecture and recitation system was abandoned and a
premium put on individual initiative on the part of the student, while the
professor became "guide, philosopher and friend" instead of lecturer or
quizzer.
The New Curriculum Plan, adopted two years ago, substituted "accom
plishment" for "time-spent" as a basis for student rating. Thus it abolished,
in effect, freshman, sophomore, junior and senior years and in their place
substituted an upper and lower division, with students devoting their first two
years mostly to generalization and the last two years mostly to specialization.
The adoption of the Unit-Cost Plan is the logical next step in the Rollins
ideal of a cultural college with a limited student body, a faculty devoted to
humanized teaching, a physical plant designed as much for beauty as
efficiency, and all adequately and scientifically financed, first, by those who
are receiving the most benefit from it, and second, by those who are able to

appreciate a genuine opportunity for wise giving.

In the death of William Vallance Hamilton on March 6, Caledonia, New
York, has lost one of its best known and most highly regarded citizens. His
life passed out early Monday morning March 6, at Strong Memorial Hospital,
Rochester, following the crash of his automobile in North Road, Wheat
land, Sunday night March 5 as he was returning home from a bank meeting
in Rochester.
A Mr. Estes, living near the scene of the accident, heard the crash, and
going there found Mr. Hamilton lying on the road, he having been thrown
from his car as it crashed against a tree. It is supposed he suffered a shock.
He was removed to Strong Memorial Hospital, where it was found he had

sustained a fractured skull. His family were summoned and were with him
when death came.
William Vallance Hamilton was the eldest son of the late William and
Jane Vallance Hamilton. He was born in this village 73 years ago and his
entire life had been spent here, where he has held a unique position in the
community. He was educated in the village schools, Peekskill Military
Academy, and Cornell University, where he was a member of the class of 1884
and also a member of the Psi Upsilon fraternity. In each of the places he
held an outstanding place for ability and intelligence.
After completing his education, he entered into partnership with his
father, under the firm name of Wm. Hamilton & Son, in the conduct of the
large produce house and banking business in this Village and the flour mill
ing business at Honeoye Falls. On the death of his father he assumed the
management of all these varied interests, carrying on in the same honest,
common-sense manner as his worthy parent. When the private bank was
merged with the First National Bank, Mr. Hamilton became its strongest asset
and continued as such throughout his life.
In local affairs Mr. Hamilton was always interested and helpful. For
years he was a member and president of the Board of Education, president
of the Water Board, served several terms as
president of the Village. At
the time of his death he was a member of the Genesee Park Commission, a
leader in Boy Scout work, an active member of the Taxpayers' League of
Livingston County. He was also a member of several clubs, Genesee Valley
Club and Elks, Rochester, Laurentian Club, the Lions, Eunice Lodge, 830,
F. & A. M., of which he was a past master. For many years he was a member
of the Livingston County Historical Society.
Mr. Hamilton was twice married, his first wife being Miss Ida Brirminstool of Henrietta, who died nearly 40 years ago. His second wife, who
survives him, was Miss Josephine Wilson of St. Louis, Mo.
Mr. Hamilton also leaves a son, Wilson Hamilton, Chi '27, who has
charge of the Honeoye Falls Bank, and a daughter, Gertrude, wife of Joseph
W. Ward of this Village, and two grandchildren, Virginia H., and Joseph
W. Ward Jr. ; a brother, J. Alexander Hamilton, New Haven, Conn. ; and a
sister, Mrs. John P. P. Lathrop, of Paoli, Pa.
Mr. Hamilton was a genial, social man, making friends easily and by
his fidelity to them, retaining their friendship. He was a student of the best
literature and was familiar with historical events, possessing a retentive mem
ory and a faculty of expression which made him an excellent public speaker.
He was a life-long Democrat and was influential in the affairs of his
party.

Lieut. Col. Alfred Fellows Masury, Sigma '04
Lieut. Col. Alfred Fellows Masury of the Army Reserve Corps, one of
the guest passengers on the Akron, died in the fatal accident of this airship
on April 4. He was vice president, chief engineer and director of the Mack
International Motor Truck Corporation, 25 Broadway, New York. He niade
the flight, according to John Sloan, his secretary, at the invitation of Rear
Admiral William A. Moffett.
Colonel Masury's flight in the Akron was not his first. Deeply interested
in aeronautics, he was a lighter-than-air enthusiast and had previously flown
thousands of miles in all kinds and types of dirigibles. He was aboard the

Graf Zeppelin on its attempted westward transatlantic flight in May, 1929,
which nearly ended disastrously.
As a passenger on that flight Colonel Masury spent six hours of anxiety
while the Zeppelin hung helplessly over France with five of her six engines
dead. Tossed by sixty-mile-an-hour winds, the crew in charge of Dr. Hugo
Eckener, the commander, landed the dirigible near Toulon.
Colonel Masury, who was 50 years old, was born in Danvers, Mass.,
the son of Charles Henry and Evelyn Fellows Masury. He attended Brown
University in Providence, being graduated from there in 1904 with an M.E.
degree.
During and after the war he worked in an advisory capacity for the
Army Ordnance Department, chiefly in connection with automotive equip
ment and transportation. Colonel Masury got his rank of Lieutenant Colonel
in the reserves, his secretary explained, by virtue of a five-year appointment
made by President Roosevelt. His body was recovered after the accident and
according to his often expressed wish, his ashes were "scattered to the four
winds," at sea.

Kennedy L. Potter, Phi '02
Brother Potter and his wife were killed in a motor accident on May 27,
near Parma, Michigan, when their car struck a parked trailer. His home was
in Jackson, Michigan.
Mr. and Mrs. Potter were returning from Albion where they had attended
a dinner party.
One mile west of Parma they crashed into the trailer which
had been parked on the highway to repair a tire. It was in charge of Clarence
York, of Detroit, who claims that three warning flares had been set out as
warnings.
Mr. and Mrs. Potter were alone in their car. It struck the trailer
squarely, throwing Mrs. Potter out on the highway and pinning Mr. Potter in
the front seat. Both were dead by the time York reached them, he told officers.
The car was demolished.
As president of the Jackson City Bank and Trust company Mr. Potter
was one of the outstanding citizens of the community. He was 55. Two sons,

George, Phi '29, and Neil, Phi '32; two brothers, Nathan S. Potter Jr., Phi '98,
of Ann Arbor and Clark Z. Potter, of Jackson, and a sister, Mrs. Harriett
C. Stewart, of Cincinnati, survive.
Graduating from the University of Michigan law school, Mr. Potter came
to Jackson to enter the banking business with his father, the late Nathan

Potter, then head of the Jackson City bank. He arose to the rank of vice
president in 1919, and last December was elected president upon the death of
William M. Thompson.
As a youth Mr. Potter served in the war with Spain, and when this country
entered the World War he again answered the call to arms. He concluded his
World War services with the rank of major. Since the war he was unusually
active in the American Legion, serving the Richard F. Smith Post No. 29
as finance officer for a number of years.
Politics played an important part in his life and several years ago he
served as chairman of the state central committee of the Republican party.
He always took a keen interest in political affairs and whether in the actual
campaign battles or not, his advice on political affairs was eagerly sought
from all parts of state.
Banker, lawyer, war veteran, one who had tasted the bitter and sweet of
political powers, Kennedy L. Potter, who was killed May 27, was probably
better known than any other man in this section of the state.
Elevated to the office of president of the Jackson City Bank and Trust
Company which he had managed for several years as vice president, Mr.

permission toopen the bank he headed; his statements to the public during
those times, will long be remembered by those who knew him well. And

He was a central figure in the meetings of bankers throughout the state

When it was learned that the Union and Peoples National Bank was not

Dr. Robert D. Sheppard, 87, a distinguished historian and former trus

securing an M.A. degree in 1872. He was a member of Phi Beta Kappa.
Northwestern made him an honorary M.A. in 1875. He subsequently was

Evanston, 111., and held pastorates in the Methodist Episcopal church in
Aurora, 111., and at the Michigan Avenue, Western Avenue and Grace churches
in Chicago.
In 1878 he was elected a trustee of Northwestern university and in 1884
to the board of the Garrett institute. He resigned his pastorate in 1884 when
elected head of the department of history and political economy at North
western. In 1892 he was elected treasurer and business
manager of North
western, serving to 1904. He was also treasurer of Garrett institute and
presi
